strengths: The paper addresses a useful and underexplored problem: jointly synthesizing mixed-type covariates, observed follow-up times, and event indicators for survival analysis. Adapting mixed-type diffusion to this setting and adding survival-oriented supervision is practically relevant and moderately original.

The method is presented with a generally clear high-level decomposition into continuous diffusion, categorical masked diffusion, and a Cox-style auxiliary objective. The manuscript and figures are visually polished. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/1b59d79faf9242b4838d942a8144cdf4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation covers three public medical datasets with substantially different censoring rates, five generative baselines, multiple downstream survival learners, ten random seeds, and several types of metrics. The reported results show credible improvements over SurvivalGAN and strong Jensen-Shannon distances.
The appendix provides dataset descriptions, major training hyperparameters, computational hardware and runtime, additional survival metrics, reduced-sample experiments, and training curves.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method preserves the censoring mechanism is not supported by either the formulation or evaluation. The paper conflates latent event time, latent censoring time, and observed follow-up time T; standard survival data instead observe min(event time, censoring time) and an indicator. Generating the observed pair (T,E) does not identify or reproduce the censoring mechanism. Moreover, the proposed survival loss uses real T and E only to construct a Cox objective from denoised covariates; it does not directly constrain generated censoring times or indicators. No conditional censoring-rate, censoring-distribution, or dependence diagnostic is reported.

There are serious mathematical specification errors. In Eq. 10, the Cox denominator sums exp(r_i) rather than exp(r_j), making the written objective incorrect. Eq. 4 uses an identity of dimension d_cont even though z concatenates d_cont covariates and T. The paper also says Cox risk sets are computed during minibatch training without explaining how full risk sets are retained; naively replacing them with within-batch risk sets does not implement the stated partial likelihood. These issues prevent reliable verification of the method.

No ablation isolates the contribution of the survival loss, sparsity-aware weighting, adaptive scaling, or joint generation. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that the proposed survival-specific components cause the gains over TabDiff. This is especially important because the architecture is largely inherited from TabDiff and the main methodological novelty is the auxiliary loss.

Several conclusions overstate the tables. SURVDIFF is not consistently best in Wasserstein distance: TVAE is better on AIDS and METABRIC, and TabDiff is also slightly better on METABRIC. TabDiff is slightly better on METABRIC C-index and Brier score. In Table 7, SURVDIFF loses to TabDiff or SurvivalGAN on AIDS RMST, AIDS KM-MSE, GBSG2 KM-MSE, and METABRIC RMST, sometimes by large factors. Thus the evidence supports competitiveness and improvements over SurvivalGAN, not consistent state-of-the-art survival fidelity.

The downstream protocol is underspecified and potentially affected by leakage. It is unclear whether the generator is fitted only on a training split and whether TSTR evaluation uses a strictly held-out real test set. Results average five heterogeneous downstream learners into a single number, without per-learner results, a train-real/test-real reference ceiling, statistical tests, or confidence intervals for method differences. This makes both practical effect size and statistical reliability difficult to assess.

Covariate fidelity is insufficiently defined: the manuscript does not explain how per-feature JS and Wasserstein distances are normalized and aggregated across mixed feature types. t-SNE plots provide weak evidence and can be highly sensitive to preprocessing and embedding choices. There is also no assessment of joint dependencies, subgroup fidelity, rare-category coverage, or memorization.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the hyperparameter tables. No code or repository is supplied, and essential quantities such as tau, the decay alpha, lambda_max, epsilon, network widths, preprocessing, split construction, synthetic cohort size, hyperparameter-selection procedure, and exact metric horizons are missing. Baseline tuning fairness is also unclear.

The paper contains no substantive limitations or ethics discussion. For synthetic clinical data, distributional similarity and downstream utility do not establish privacy; membership-inference, nearest-neighbor, or disclosure-risk evaluation is absent. Potential subgroup harms, misuse of synthetic records, and the implications of downweighting late events—which may systematically reduce fidelity for long survivors—are not discussed. These omissions materially weaken the claimed clinical applicability.

strengths: Significance: Synthetic survival data is an important problem, and jointly generating mixed-type covariates, observed follow-up times, and event indicators is potentially useful.

Originality: Adding survival-oriented supervision to a mixed-type diffusion model is a reasonable idea, and the proposed late-event weighting is intuitively motivated, although the contribution is incremental.
Evidence: The study includes three real medical datasets, several generative baselines, five downstream survival learners, ten-seed summaries, and a reduced-sample analysis.
Presentation: The high-level motivation and model pipeline are generally understandable, and the appendix reports computational requirements and many hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation (10) is not the Cox partial likelihood described in the text. Its denominator uses exp(r_i) for every member of the risk set rather than exp(r_j). Taken literally, the ratio reduces to 1/|R(t_i)|, making the purported survival loss constant with respect to the model. If this is only a typographical error, the central method is still not reproducible from the manuscript. Soundness: The central claim of preserving the censoring mechanism is not established. The method generates the observed time and event indicator but does not separately model latent event and censoring times; the auxiliary Cox loss concerns event-risk ordering and does not directly constrain the conditional censoring distribution. No conditional censoring-rate or dependence evaluation is provided.

Evidence: The survival-specific results contradict the broad superiority claims. In Table 7, SURVDIFF is best on only two of six dataset-metric combinations; TabDiff is substantially better on GBSG2 KM MSE (0.0005 versus 0.0062) and METABRIC RMST gap (0.0048 versus 0.0268), while SurvivalGAN is better on AIDS KM MSE.

Evidence: No ablation isolates the survival loss, sparsity weighting, or adaptive scaling, despite the manuscript claiming ablation evidence against naive tabular diffusion. Consequently, improvements over TabDiff cannot be attributed to the proposed components.

Evaluation validity: The paper does not clearly specify a held-out real test set. If the generator is trained on all real records and TSTR is evaluated on those same records, downstream results are vulnerable to memorization and do not measure generalization. A real-data training upper bound is also absent.

Reproducibility: Essential details are missing or inconsistent, including tau and the decay alpha in Equation (11), lambda_max and epsilon, preprocessing, synthetic sample count, Brier-score evaluation horizons, RMST horizon, distance aggregation, data-split protocol, and per-downstream-model results. The continuous-state covariance dimension also appears inconsistent because z includes time but Equation (4) uses I_dcont.

Originality and significance: The technical contribution is largely TabDiff plus a weighted Cox auxiliary head. Without a correct objective, ablations, or convincing censoring evaluation, the claimed first tailored diffusion model does not yet amount to a reliable advance. Validation is limited to three small public datasets and excludes controlled simulations with known censoring mechanisms, dependent censoring, competing risks, and time-varying covariates.

Research ethics and limitations: The clinical-data motivation repeatedly invokes data accessibility, but no privacy or disclosure-risk evaluation is conducted. Synthetic fidelity does not imply privacy. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering memorization, proportional-hazards assumptions, informative censoring, or possible bias from deliberately downweighting late events.

Presentation: Several claims are overstated relative to the tables, and the notation blurs observed follow-up time, latent event time, and censoring time. The manuscript also does not explain clearly how the noise-prediction output is converted into the denoised covariates consumed by the survival head. These issues obstruct verification of the central method.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: jointly synthesizing mixed-type covariates, observed follow-up times, and event indicators for survival analysis. The end-to-end formulation is practically appealing. SURVDIFF combines a strong mixed-type tabular diffusion backbone with survival supervision and an intuitively motivated weighting scheme for late events. This is a sensible extension of TabDiff, even if the methodological novelty is moderate.

The evaluation includes three real medical datasets with substantially different censoring rates, five downstream survival learners, several generative baselines, ten random seeds, and a small-sample sensitivity analysis.

The reported results are promising: SURVDIFF has the best Jensen-Shannon distance on all three datasets, generally improves TSTR C-index and Brier score over SurvivalGAN, and performs particularly well on the highly censored AIDS dataset.
The paper is generally readable and supplies architecture, optimization, hardware, runtime, and baseline hyperparameter information in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving the censoring mechanism is not established. The method generates the observed tuple (X,T,E), where T is defined as either an event or censoring time, but the manuscript then treats T as a conventional survival time when defining S(t|x). Without assumptions separating latent event and censoring times, matching the observed joint distribution does not identify or demonstrate recovery of the underlying censoring mechanism.

The proposed survival loss does not directly constrain generated times or event indicators: its risk score is computed from denoised covariates, while true T and E only define the Cox risk sets. The paper does not explain why this auxiliary prediction loss should ensure fidelity of generated (T,E), and it provides no ablation isolating the survival loss, sparsity weighting, or adaptive scaling from the TabDiff backbone.

Equation (10) appears technically incorrect: its denominator is written as a sum of exp(r_i), rather than exp(r_j) over j in the risk set. As written, the risk scores cancel and the objective cannot train the survival head. If this is merely a typographical error, the implemented objective and code are still needed to verify the reported method.

The survival-specific evidence is mixed and does not support the paper's repeated claims of consistent superiority. In Table 7, SURVDIFF is best on only two of six dataset-metric combinations; TabDiff has a better RMST gap on AIDS and METABRIC, while SurvivalGAN has a lower KM MSE on AIDS and TabDiff is much better on GBSG2. The paper characterizes these results as broadly comparable without analyzing the failures.

Evaluation details needed to rule out optimistic TSTR results are missing. The manuscript does not clearly specify real-data train/test splits, whether the generator ever sees downstream test records, synthetic sample counts, preprocessing, Brier-score horizons and censoring correction, or tuning/selection protocols. Results are averaged across five heterogeneous downstream models, concealing per-model behavior, and no real-data-trained upper bound or statistical comparison is reported.

Covariate fidelity is assessed mainly through marginal JS/Wasserstein summaries and t-SNE plots. These do not adequately test multivariate dependence, conditional survival relationships, rare categories, subgroup fidelity, or memorization. The visual evidence is especially weak because t-SNE proximity is not a reliable distributional test.

Originality is limited: the main construction is a TabDiff-style mixed-data diffusion model augmented with a weighted Cox auxiliary loss. The novelty could still be useful, but the absence of component ablations makes it impossible to attribute improvements to the survival-specific contributions.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the hyperparameter tables: no code or availability statement is provided, key data-processing and evaluation choices are unspecified, and the apparent error in the main objective creates implementation ambiguity.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion. For synthetic clinical data, privacy leakage and membership or attribute inference are material concerns, yet no privacy evaluation or guarantee is provided. Potential bias amplification, subgroup harms, dependence on proportional-hazards supervision, and the danger of treating synthetic records as clinically valid are also not discussed.
